reverse_outline.summary: A balance is a debt record, valid only while an outside record agrees, and every status is one party's reversible statement at a moment
Larkfield's books showed €412,000 more owed to studios than its providers' balances, despite every payment status being right, traced to post-payout refunds, chargeback fees and a rounding rule
A payment's state machine cannot hold that difference because it does not record who owes whom, which needs a second record and a way to prove it

Part III's claim: a provider knows where money is only from its own double-entry ledger matched against outside records, with balances, payouts and licenses as views of that ledger / the reader should give up the view that money is simply 'at the provider' like cash in a bank
Five chapters answer five dependent questions, ledger first because everything is read from it and licenses last because safeguarding is one more ledger-to-bank comparison

The ledgers chapter shows a provider knows whose money it holds from immutable balanced entries and clearing accounts, enforced at write (Adyen) or checked afterwards (Stripe), replayed on Larkfield's €412,000

The balances chapter shows a merchant's balance is a claim on the provider whose pending/available/reserved states are the provider's payment decisions, contrasting Adyen and Stripe, with Mila's €120 pass as the case
The payouts chapter shows 'paid' only means sent and a failed transfer returns days later as a new credit, as in Larkfield's 412 bounced payouts

The reconciliation chapter shows a provider proves its books by matching against records others wrote and gives customers scheduled reports, from which they should write their books rather than from webhooks
The licences chapter shows only a licensed institution may hold customer money, compares Stripe's and Adyen's status, and uses Larkfield's stopped proposal to hold payouts itself
A reader with a specific problem should go straight to the chapter that owns that symptom

Otherwise read in order, since all five chapters ask what a record says is owed and whose independent record agrees / that question explains the opening: the €412,000 sat in post-payment movements a payment record has no place for

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

The cold reader named the five chapters' subjects in reading order (ledgers; balances and funds flows; payouts; reconciliation and reporting; licences and safeguarding), gave the stated reason the ledger comes first, and predicted the kinds of evidence and the tone.

The cold reader answered: from a double-entry ledger the provider keeps itself, matched against records it did not write (network files, bank statements); not from a payment's status and not from a dashboard balance. This equals the expected answer.
All eleven prose units match the controlling idea of the spec paragraph they are aligned to, in spec order; the KEY POINTS callout matches the callout evidence of p03.

The outliner marked Introduction ¶3 and Where to Begin ¶2. In ¶3 the view to give up is the claim stated in the negative, as p03 declares; in Where to Begin ¶2 the common question is what explains the opening, as p11 declares. Each is one idea.
Each chapter paragraph introduces the chapter arguing one of P3-1 to P3-5; the introduction and closing paragraphs state or frame the part thesis.

Both figures carry a caption that says what they show; the opening scenario is explained by the next paragraph; the chapter cases are named as the chapters' contents, each after the statement it illustrates.

results.quote: asks last **who is legally allowed to hold customer money, and where it sits**
results.finding: The boundary is marked only by 'last', a sequence marker. The declared elaboration is not expressed and the declared known information (reconciliation as a comparison between a ledger and a bank's record) is not picked up; the paragraph never ties the license question to that comparison.

results.quote: The rest of the part is that ledger seen from one side at a time.
results.finding: Both flow readers stopped to count the 'sides': the sentence names balance, report, payout and license, Figure 1 groups them differently and adds the outside records, and the next paragraph gives five chapters; neither could settle how the sides map onto the chapters. (Reader A alone also found the 'view to give up' sentence out of place after the map of the part.)
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item B3 (flow reader A, item A1)

results.quote: Licenses come last because safeguarding, the legal duty to keep customers' money apart from the firm's own, is by then one more comparison between a ledger and a bank account, this time required by law.
results.finding: Both flow readers had to supply a missing link in the reason for the last position: reader A had to connect licensing to safeguarding, reader B re-read because reconciliation as a ledger-to-bank comparison has not been named yet and 'by then' carries the argument. Reader B (B4) and the introduction reader also note that 'each needs the one before' is justified only for the first and last chapters.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item B5 (flow reader A, item A11)

results.quote: Stripe publishes a schedule and, for standard payouts, does not say, beyond terms that let a payout wait when a network fails to pay Stripe.
results.finding: Both flow readers named this the hardest sentence on the page (reader B read it three times): 'does not say' has no object, which must be carried over from the Adyen clause before the 'beyond terms' qualification can attach. Both also misread 'the book's recurring payment' as a subscription and 'three figures' as a three-digit number in the next sentence.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, items B6 and B7 (flow reader A, items A3 and A4)

results.quote: In Larkfield's Payout That Bounced, 412 payouts worth €386,000 were returned in June 2026 to a record that had already closed them
results.finding: Both flow readers stopped to check whether the 412 payouts are the opening's €412,000 incident; the page does not say they are separate. Reader A adds that 'that amount' (Mila's €117.47) is dropped for a different case; reader B that the capitalized case name reads as already known.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item B9 (flow reader A, item A5)

results.quote: turns that case, two records of the same money that disagree, into the general question
results.finding: Both flow readers hesitated over which case 'that case' is: the gloss fits the opening €412,000 as well as the bounced payouts, and the previous paragraph did not describe the bounce as two disagreeing records. Both also could not say what 'one level down' is down from.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item B10 (flow reader A, items A6 and A7)

results.quote: refunds made after the payout (the provider's transfer of a studio's money to its bank account), fees on chargebacks (card payments reversed by the cardholder's bank after a dispute) and a currency-conversion rounding rule
results.finding: Flow reader B re-read to find the three items because two parenthetical glosses sit inside the list, and found 'its bank account' ambiguous for a moment. Reader A reported no difficulty here.

Flow reader A hesitated over the routing: an unexplained difference and a close that will not tie read as nearly the same problem, and the page has just said reconciliation is what explains a difference between records. Reader B did not report this.

Flow reader B found the return to the opening case interrupting the advice between 'Otherwise read in order' and 'Begin with', after the reader has filed the case. Reader A found the return fitting. The order is the one p11 declares.

results.quote: itemized per payout at Stripe and per payable batch at Adyen
results.finding: 'Payable batch' is used without a gloss and is not in what the audience already knows; both flow readers could not place it.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader A, item A7; flow reader B, item B10

results.quote: a close that will not tie to [[payment-reconciliation-and-reporting]]
results.finding: 'A close that will not tie' is accounting shorthand the page has not prepared (only 'It closes one Larkfield day' comes before), and the elided 'belongs' makes it read as 'will not tie to the chapter'. Both flow readers reported it. Reader B alone also notes 'funds flow' is used as a known term in the next sentence.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader A, item A8; flow reader B, item B11

results.quote: six accounts and one posting function
results.finding: 'Posting function' (and 'posting') is not explained; flow reader B reported it as guessable. Reader A did not report it.
The introduction opens on a specific scenario, bridges from Part II, states the claim and gives the roadmap; none of the weak patterns.
The conclusion gives a course of action and a synthesis; it does not open with 'in conclusion', add a subtopic, hold body evidence or end on a rephrased thesis alone.
'The five chapters ask one question five times' is stated by no single chapter paragraph; it matters because it explains the opening difference and tells the reader where to enter.
Where to Begin ¶2 returns to the opening's €412,000 and says where it sat: in movements after the payment and in a rounding rule.
